title: Business Law
objective: Explain how contracts, business ownership forms and consumer-protection rules shape everyday business decisions.
body:
Business law sets the rules every company plays by. Three ideas show up again and again on exams.

**Contracts.** A contract is a legally enforceable agreement. To be valid it needs an *offer*, *acceptance*, *consideration* (something of value exchanged by both sides), *competent parties* (of legal age and sound mind) and a *legal purpose*. Missing any one of these elements makes the agreement void or voidable. A minor can usually cancel a contract for non-necessities, which is why many businesses require a parent's signature.

**Forms of ownership.** A *sole proprietorship* is owned by one person who keeps all profits and carries unlimited personal liability. A *general partnership* splits profits, decisions and liability between two or more owners. A *corporation* is a separate legal entity, so shareholders' liability is limited to what they invested, but profits can be taxed twice. A *limited liability company (LLC)* combines limited liability with pass-through taxation.

**Regulation and protection.** Government agencies protect consumers and competition. Antitrust laws stop monopolies and price fixing. Truth-in-advertising rules ban deceptive claims. Intellectual property law protects creators: *patents* cover inventions, *copyrights* cover creative works, and *trademarks* cover brand names and logos.

When you see a law question, first ask: who is protected, and what right or duty is involved?
examples: A store owner offers to sell a used register for $300, the buyer agrees and pays: offer, acceptance and consideration are all present.
A shoe company registers its swoosh-style logo so competitors cannot copy it: that is trademark protection.

questions.stem: Which element of a contract is missing if one party promises to give a friend a laptop and expects nothing in return?
questions.explanation: Consideration means both parties exchange something of value. A one-sided gift promise has no consideration, so it is not an enforceable contract.

questions.stem: Maria owns a bakery by herself and is personally responsible for all of its debts. Which form of ownership is this?
questions.explanation: A sole proprietorship has one owner who keeps all profits and has unlimited personal liability for business debts.

questions.stem: A company invents a new battery design and wants to stop others from making it for a period of years. What should it obtain?
questions.explanation: Patents protect inventions and processes. Copyrights protect creative works and trademarks protect brand identifiers.

questions.stem: Why do many investors prefer the corporate form of ownership?
choices: It is the easiest form to start
questions.explanation: Shareholders can lose only what they invested; the corporation itself is responsible for its debts.

questions.stem: Two competing gas stations secretly agree to charge the same high price. Which type of law does this most likely violate?
questions.explanation: Price fixing reduces competition, which antitrust laws are designed to prevent.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old signs a contract to buy a $900 gaming system and later wants to cancel. What is most likely true?
choices: The minor can usually void the contract
questions.explanation: Minors generally lack contractual capacity for non-necessities, so they can usually void such contracts.

questions.stem: Which business ownership form offers limited liability while allowing profits to pass through to the owners' personal tax returns?
questions.explanation: An LLC combines the liability protection of a corporation with pass-through taxation.

flashcards.definition: Something of value that each party gives or promises in a contract.
Owners are personally responsible for all business debts, risking personal assets.
Legal protection for a word, symbol or design that identifies a brand.
Laws that promote competition by banning monopolies and practices such as price fixing.
Limited liability company: limited liability for owners with pass-through taxation.

title: Communications
objective: Choose clear, audience-appropriate messages and channels, and apply active listening in business settings.
body:
Communication is the transfer of meaning from a sender to a receiver. The basic model has a *sender* who encodes a message, a *channel* (email, meeting, phone, social media), a *receiver* who decodes it, and *feedback* that shows whether it was understood. Anything that gets in the way is *noise*: background sound, jargon, emotions or a poorly chosen channel.

**Pick the right channel.** Rich channels (face-to-face, video) carry tone and body language and suit sensitive or complex messages, like a performance conversation. Lean channels (memos, email) suit routine, factual information that people may need to keep.

**Write for the reader.** Lead with the main point, use short sentences, and end with a clear action: who does what by when. Proofread for tone, since written messages lose facial cues.

**Listen actively.** Active listening means giving full attention, asking clarifying questions and paraphrasing ("So what I'm hearing is..."). It builds trust and prevents costly misunderstandings.

**Nonverbal cues.** Eye contact, posture and gestures can support or contradict your words. In a DECA role-play, a firm handshake, steady eye contact and an organized summary are communication skills the judge notices.
examples: A manager announces layoffs in person instead of by email because the message is sensitive and employees will have questions.
An employee repeats a customer's complaint back to confirm understanding before offering a fix.

questions.stem: In the communication process, what is 'noise'?
choices: The volume of the speaker's voice
Anything that interferes with understanding the message
questions.explanation: Noise is any barrier, physical or psychological, that distorts or blocks the message.

questions.stem: Which channel is best for delivering complex, sensitive news to a team?
questions.explanation: Face-to-face is a rich channel that allows tone, body language and immediate questions.

questions.stem: Paraphrasing what a speaker said is an example of:
questions.explanation: Paraphrasing confirms understanding and shows the speaker you are paying attention.

questions.stem: What should usually come first in a business email?
questions.explanation: Busy readers need the purpose immediately; supporting details follow.

questions.stem: Feedback in the communication process tells the sender:
questions.explanation: Feedback closes the loop by showing how the receiver interpreted the message.

questions.stem: A salesperson crosses their arms and looks away while saying 'I'm happy to help.' What is the likely effect?
questions.explanation: Closed posture and poor eye contact signal disinterest, undermining the spoken message.

questions.stem: Using technical terms a customer does not know is an example of which barrier?
questions.explanation: Jargon is specialized language that confuses receivers outside the field.

flashcards.definition: Fully concentrating, asking questions and paraphrasing to confirm understanding.
Any barrier that interferes with a message being received as intended.
The medium used to send a message, such as email, phone or a meeting.
The receiver's response that shows how a message was understood.
Messages sent through body language, facial expressions, gestures and tone.

title: Customer Relations
objective: Use service techniques that build loyalty and resolve complaints in a way that keeps customers coming back.
body:
Keeping a customer is usually far cheaper than winning a new one, so businesses invest in *customer relations*: every interaction that shapes how customers feel about the company.

**Know what customers expect.** Customers want reliability (doing what you promised), responsiveness (prompt help), assurance (knowledgeable, courteous staff), empathy (individual attention) and tangibles (clean, professional surroundings).

**Handle complaints with a process.** A widely taught approach is: *listen* without interrupting, *empathize* ("I understand how frustrating that is"), *apologize* for the experience, *solve* the problem or offer options, and *follow up*. Never argue or blame the customer. A complaint handled well can create a more loyal customer than one who never had a problem.

**Build loyalty.** Loyalty programs, personalized service and remembering preferences encourage repeat business. *Customer relationship management (CRM)* systems store purchase history and preferences so employees can personalize each interaction.

**Brand promise.** Every employee represents the brand. Consistent service across locations and channels (in-store, phone, online) keeps the brand promise believable.
examples: A hotel clerk apologizes for a noisy room, moves the guest immediately and sends a complimentary breakfast voucher.
A coffee shop's app remembers a customer's usual order and offers a reward after 10 visits.

questions.stem: What is usually the FIRST step when handling an upset customer's complaint?
questions.explanation: Listening first shows respect and helps you understand the real problem before responding.

questions.stem: Why do businesses focus on keeping existing customers?
choices: It is usually cheaper than attracting new customers
questions.explanation: Acquisition costs such as advertising make new customers expensive; loyal customers also tend to spend more over time.

questions.stem: A CRM system primarily helps a business:
choices: Store and use customer information to personalize service
questions.explanation: Customer relationship management software tracks interactions and preferences.

questions.stem: Saying 'I understand how frustrating that must be' demonstrates:
questions.explanation: Empathy means recognizing and acknowledging the customer's feelings.

questions.stem: Which action most directly supports a company's brand promise?
choices: Changing service standards at each location
Delivering consistent service across all channels
questions.explanation: Consistency makes the brand's promise believable wherever customers interact with it.

questions.stem: An employee who arrives on time for every scheduled delivery is demonstrating which service quality?
questions.explanation: Reliability means consistently doing what was promised.

questions.stem: After resolving a complaint, what step helps confirm the customer is satisfied?
choices: Offering a survey to a different customer
questions.explanation: Follow-up shows ongoing care and catches any remaining issues.

flashcards.definition: All activities a business uses to build positive, lasting relationships with customers.
Customer relationship management: systems and practices for tracking and personalizing customer interactions.
A customer's tendency to keep buying from the same business.
The consistent experience a company commits to delivering to customers.
Understanding and acknowledging a customer's feelings.

title: Economics
objective: Apply supply and demand, scarcity and economic systems to explain how prices and business decisions are made.
body:
Economics studies how people and businesses make choices with limited resources.

**Scarcity and opportunity cost.** Resources (land, labor, capital, entrepreneurship) are limited while wants are unlimited, so every choice has an *opportunity cost*: the value of the next-best alternative you give up.

**Supply and demand.** The *law of demand* says that as price rises, quantity demanded falls. The *law of supply* says that as price rises, producers supply more. The *equilibrium price* is where the two meet. A shortage (demand greater than supply) pushes prices up; a surplus pushes prices down. Demand shifts when income, tastes, the price of related goods or expectations change.

**Elasticity.** If demand is *elastic*, a small price change causes a big change in quantity demanded (luxury items, products with many substitutes). If demand is *inelastic*, quantity barely changes (gasoline, medicine).

**Economic systems.** In a *market* economy, individuals and businesses answer what, how and for whom to produce. In a *command* economy, the government decides. Most countries, including the U.S., are *mixed* economies.

**Measuring the economy.** *GDP* measures total output, *inflation* is a general rise in prices, and the *business cycle* moves through expansion, peak, contraction and trough.
examples: Concert tickets sell out within minutes and resale prices soar: demand exceeds supply at the original price.
A student who chooses to work a shift instead of attending a review session gives up the review session as the opportunity cost.

questions.stem: What is opportunity cost?
choices: The price paid for a product
The value of the next-best alternative given up
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is what you sacrifice when you choose one option over another.

questions.stem: If the price of a product rises and nothing else changes, what happens to quantity demanded?
questions.explanation: The law of demand states that price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions.

questions.stem: A shortage occurs when:
choices: Supply exceeds demand at the current price
Demand exceeds supply at the current price
questions.explanation: When more people want a product than is available at a price, a shortage results and prices tend to rise.

questions.stem: Demand for which product is most likely inelastic?
questions.explanation: Necessities with few substitutes keep similar demand even when prices rise.

questions.stem: The United States is best described as which type of economy?
questions.explanation: The U.S. is mostly market-driven but includes government regulation and public services.

questions.stem: Which phase of the business cycle features falling output and rising unemployment?
questions.explanation: During a contraction (or recession), economic activity declines.

questions.stem: A general, sustained rise in the price level is called:
questions.explanation: Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money.

flashcards.definition: Limited resources compared with unlimited wants, forcing choices.
The price at which quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
Demand that changes a lot when price changes, often due to many substitutes.
An economy combining market decisions with government involvement.
Gross domestic product: the total value of goods and services produced in a country.
